name: PixelLab
tagline: AI generator for pixel art characters, sprites, tilesets and frame-by-frame animation, with editor plugins.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The parts that look like the product are the easy parts: a prompt box, palette quantization, nearest-neighbour downscale, sprite sheet export. All of that is a weekend of Python. The part you cannot reproduce is a model actually tuned to emit clean pixel grids, consistent characters across 4 or 8 rotations, and inbetween animation frames that hold the same silhouette. Generic Stable Diffusion plus a pixel-art LoRA gives you pixel-ish art: blurry grids, drifting palettes, a character who grows a new hat between frames. You can build a fun local sprite toy, you cannot build the animation pipeline, and that is the whole reason people pay.
coreLoopDIY: Local Gradio app that runs a pixel-art LoRA over SDXL, snaps output to a fixed palette and pixel grid, and exports transparent PNGs plus a sprite sheet.
requirements: an NVIDIA GPU with 12GB+ VRAM, or a rented one
a Hugging Face token for model weights
patience for background removal on dark sprites
whatYouLose: Rotation sets: the same character viewed from 4 or 8 angles without redrawing itself
Skeleton and inbetween animation, which is the actual product
Character consistency across a batch, so your walk cycle is eight different characters
Aseprite, Godot and Figma plugin integration, so everything round-trips through your downloads folder
Genuinely clean pixel grids instead of upscaled mush with a palette filter on top
moatNotes: Fine-tuning a diffusion model to respect a pixel grid and keep a character identical across animation frames is the hard research, and it is not in any public checkpoint you can pull down.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because game artists do not want pixel-art-flavoured illustrations, they want assets that drop into an engine: fixed canvas size, fixed palette, transparent background, consistent character across every frame and every facing direction. Hitting that reliably is a model problem, not a UI problem, and the open checkpoints are not there yet. The editor plugins matter too: an asset that needs ten minutes of manual cleanup per frame is worse than no asset at all. A local build is a decent idea generator for mockups and placeholder art, which is a real use, just not the paid one.
notes: You can clone the palette snapping and the export formats in an afternoon. The moat is a model fine-tuned to keep one character identical across eight rotations and twelve frames, and nothing you can download does that.
prompt:
Build a local pixel-art sprite generator. Stack: Python 3.11, diffusers, Pillow, Gradio. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

In scope:
1. Load SDXL base plus a pixel-art LoRA from Hugging Face (make the LoRA repo id a config value so I can swap it).
2. Gradio UI with: prompt, negative prompt, seed, target sprite size (16, 32, 48, 64), palette size (8, 16, 32), and a batch count.
3. Generation pipeline, in this order: generate at 1024x1024, crop to square, nearest-neighbour downscale to the target size, snap colors to a palette using median-cut quantization at the chosen palette size, then nearest-neighbour upscale to a 512px preview so I can actually see it.
4. Background removal: flood fill from the four corners with a color tolerance slider, write alpha, keep a toggle to skip it.
5. Palette lock: let me upload a PNG, extract its unique colors, and quantize all future output to that exact palette instead of median-cut.
6. Export: individual transparent PNGs at true sprite size, plus a horizontal sprite sheet of the batch with a JSON metadata file (frame width, height, count).
7. Local gallery: every generation writes to ./out/TIMESTAMP/ with the full params in params.json so I can reproduce a seed.

Out of scope, do not attempt: rotation sets, skeleton rigging, animation inbetweening, tileset auto-tiling, editor plugins. Say so in the README.

Secrets: HF_TOKEN in .env, read with python-dotenv, .env in .gitignore. Model weights cache to ./models.

Ship: app.py, pipeline.py, palette.py, requirements.txt, README.md with GPU VRAM requirements and a one-command run. Default to CPU with a loud warning if no CUDA device is found. No tests, no Docker.
